newsitem.title: USA: Is a currency board the right thing for Bulgaria?.
newsitem.headline: Is a currency board the right thing for Bulgaria?.

text.p: As Bulgaria considered putting in place a currency board, some U.S. economists warned that, far from being a panacea, such a board cannot take the place of sound macroeconomic policy.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) proposed that Bulgaria implement a currency board -- which would strictly match money in circulation to the level of hard currency reserves -- to curb inflation, and stabilize the currency and financial markets.

But Bulgaria's problems do not stem from the typical target of a currency board: runaway prices triggered by inflationary monetary policy, said Eric Neilsen, senior economist at Goldman, Sachs and Co Inc.
Bulgaria's bloated state enterprises and the strains they imposed on the banking system destabilized the economy, but the problems did not necessitate a currency board, analysts said.
"If you don't address those (problems) it's not going to work with or without a currency board," Neilsen said. "If you do those things, you don't really need a currency board."
Bulgaria's crisis of confidence intensified last week as Bulgarians clamored to convert their savings into dollars, forcing the lev 30 percent lower.
Depositors have swamped the State Savings Bank, the nation's largest savings institution, spooking panic across Bulgaria's financial markets.
Currency boards have been put in place in Hong Kong, Lithuania, Estonia and Argentina, providing economic stability, but also bringing other problems.

ING Barings said in a November 15 research report that a currency board could restore confidence in the lev and force a rapid restructuring of the industrial and banking sectors, but might leave the country exposed to potential external shocks, over-reliance on external capital and an overvalued currency.

Guillermo Calvo, an economics professor at the University of Maryland who forecast Mexico's 1994 financial crisis, said Bulgaria was on a path to repeat the inflationary policies of Latin America during the 1980s.
He questioned, however, whether a currency board would be the correct medicine for Bulgaria.

"What Bulgaria has to do is to lower interest rates and have a big explosion of wages, prices and exchange rates, to kill off money once and for all," he said, suggesting the strategy employed during Poland's stabilization.
Now that the IMF has spoken openly about a currency board, the country may have no alternative to its implementation, if only to restore confidence.
"Now the train has left the station and the Fund has talked about it, it is the right thing to do," Neilsen said.
But other economists argue that, given the country's poor track record on economic liberalization, Bulgaria would benefit from the strictures of the plan.

"They just don't have institutions set up that are strong enough to allow for either monetary or fiscal discipline," said Johns Hopkins University Professor Steve Hanke. "These (currency board) systems simply put so much discipline in the economy." -- 212-859-1671
